messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 72

**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 42-year-old married South Asian man who presents for therapy at the urging of his wife. He is a tax inspector for the federal government, a job he has held for sixteen years. He arrives to his sessions dressed in pressed, dark slacks and a collared shirt, but his posture is collapsed, and his eyes rarely meet mine. He speaks with a quiet, deliberate precision, as if he is still trying to file away his own experience into the wrong ledger.

The event that changed him occurred eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. Mr. A. was driving home from a routine audit at a small business. He recalls the day as unremarkable—clear skies, light traffic. He was stopped at a red light, his mind half on a discrepancy in the client’s inventory reports. When the light turned green, he accelerated normally. He did not see the man. The man was crossing against the signal, stepping between stopped cars. Mr. A. felt the thud before he understood what had happened. He remembers the sound of his own brakes, the screech, and then the silence. He got out of his car. The man was on the ground, his leg bent at an angle that Mr. A. still sees in his mind every single night. The man was conscious, groaning. Mr. A. knelt beside him, his hands shaking, and he kept saying, “I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I didn’t see you.” The ambulance came. The man survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and a shattered femur. He will likely never walk normally again.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. A. tried to return to his life. He went back to work, but the numbers no longer made sense to him. He sits at his desk, staring at spreadsheets, but the columns blur. He cannot concentrate. He finds himself replaying the thud, the angle of the leg, the sound of the man’s breathing. His supervisor has noticed his errors—miscalculations in tax liabilities, missed deadlines. Mr. A. has been placed on a performance improvement plan. He tells me he feels like he is drowning in a job he once mastered.

At home, he is a ghost. His wife, Priya, tells him she feels like she is living with a stranger. He no longer eats dinner with her. He sits alone in the dark living room, watching the headlights of cars pass on the street. He has stopped driving entirely. He takes the bus to work, a route that adds an hour to his commute, because the thought of sitting behind the wheel makes his heart race and his palms sweat. He avoids intersections. He avoids crosswalks. He once walked three miles out of his way to avoid the specific street where it happened.

He has not slept through the night since the accident. He wakes at 3:00 AM, drenched in sweat, the image of the man’s leg burned into his vision. He tries to tell himself it was an accident, that the man was jaywalking, that the light was green. But the logic does not stick. He believes, with a certainty that feels like a physical weight in his chest, that he is a bad person. He replays the moment—*I should have looked harder. I should have seen him. I am a killer.* The thought loops, and he cannot stop it.

He has stopped seeing his friends. He stopped going to the temple with his family. He feels a deep, corrosive shame. He tells me he does not deserve to feel better. When I ask him what he expects from therapy, he looks at the floor and says, “I don’t know. I just want the pictures to stop.” He says this without hope, as if he knows the request is impossible.
